https://www.politico.eu/article/french-p.text: PARIS — Officials working for French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu have met with banking executives to explore ways to ease financing issues faced by the National Rally and other parties ahead of next year’s presidential election. An aide from the prime minister’s office, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive issues, told reporters that officials discussed ways to help politicians get bank loans to finance their presidential campaigns. One option on the table is a loan agreed between several banks and including a partial state guarantee. In France, unlike the US and other European countries, political donations for election campaigns are strictly capped, and presidential candidates depend on bank loans to finance campaigns, which are then partially refunded by the state. Advertisement Advertisement Far-right leader Marine Le Pen has often struggled to secure a loan despite heading one of the most popular parties in France, with banks wary of perceived reputational damage that comes with financing the far right. “It’s essential that all the candidates, whatever their political creed, can access French funding to finance their campaign,” said the aide from the prime minister’s office. Lecornu’s initiative aims to avoid the interference of a “foreign financing network.” In the past, the National Rally has obtained loans from Russian and Hungarian banks. A person close to Lecornu, also granted anonymity to speak freely, however, said that the prime minister’s office was not “negotiating on behalf” of the far right. “It’s as false as it is absurd. We are opponents, and there have been no discussions between the PM’s office and the National Rally on the subject,” the person said. The initiative would also benefit other smaller candidates. Victor Goury-Laffont contributed to this report. Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: Joe Sohm/Visions of America/Universal Images Group/Getty Images Alaska Alaska athlete uses bear spray to fend off animal attack: ‘nightmare come to life’ Klaire Rhodes was attacked by a brown bear in state park but spray helped her escape with ‘relatively minor injuries’ Ramon Antonio Vargas Wed 19 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 06.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Alaska marathon athlete used a repellant spray to fend off an attacking bear that officials say injured her while she ran on a popular trail recently – an encounter that she has since described as “a nightmare come to life”. The particularly harrowing episode unfolded on 13 August, when a woman who later identified herself online as marathon winner Klaire Rhodes, 28, was running alone on the Wolverine Bowl trail in Chugach state park, officials with Alaska’s fish and game department said . A brown bear on the trail attacked and injured her, according to the agency. She was equipped with bear spray and deployed the irritant on the animal to halt the attack – before “self-rescuing” to the Prospect Heights trailhead in the city of Anchorage. The runner was then brought to a local hospital for treatment, officials said. Biologists interviewed her and went to the attack site to look for signs of the bear, but didn’t find any. They said they then posted warning signs at the trailhead while also reminding visitors to – among other things – carry deterrents such as bear spray. Fish and game department officials didn’t name Rhodes in their statement on the incident. But on Sunday, she wrote in a social media post that she had been the attacked runner, adding: “I … feel incredibly fortunate that I came out of the situation with relatively minor injuries.” Rhodes said the “most severe” of those was “a deep puncture wound” to her left hip as well as “claw and teeth marks” on her body. “At risk of sounding dramatic but being totally honest, the moment felt like a nightmare come to life,” the professional runner’s post continued. “And yes, bear spray works.” Rhodes recounted how “running in the Chugach is where I feel most at home”. Alluding to the bear whose path crossed with hers, she said: “It just so happens to also be someone else’s home, too, and despite all the precautions in the world, it’s just a risk to live life in the way we love.” She also remarked, “The outcome was just about as good as it could have been, and I’m actually really proud of how I handled a completely terrifying situation.” Having won three consecutive Mount Marathon races, as reported by the Anchorage Daily News , Rhodes said she had been preparing to race in Europe “in less than two weeks”. She said she was unsure what the attack meant for her race preparations. And she explained having mixed feelings about being able to get back to racing soon and simultaneously grappling with anxiety at the thought of again “running in the woods”. “Strange to feel overwhelmed with gratitude to be OK and knowing I probably have some intense trauma to work through,” Rhodes wrote. Alaska wildlife officials estimate that hundreds of thousands of bears inhabit the state. They calculate that some areas may have one bear every square mile. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Two US army soldiers injured by brown bear during training exercise in Alaska Read more The attack on Rhodes came roughly four months after a brown bear injured two US army soldiers in a mountainous training area at the Elmendorf-Richardson base in Anchorage. A brown bear on 9 July then mauled a resident of the city of Kenai after climbing – with two cubs – over a fence into her front yard, Alaska’s public safety department reported . Nine days later, Anchorage police said, a bear attacked and injured a woman who was hiking with a friend and three dogs. A study by the state of Alaska’s epidemiology section, meanwhile, counted at least 68 people who were hospitalized in connection with bear attacks during a 17-year period beginning in 2000. Nearly all of the attacks in the study were by brown bears. Neither authorities nor Rhodes provided specifics about the bear attack that victimized her. Although she said she was grateful for an outpouring of moral support she had received as word of the attack spread, she said she refused to “rehash” its details online “because the internet is a weird place with a lot of unsolicited opinions”. “I might share the full story another time, which I know will open a can of worms of opinions on what I did or didn’t do wrong,” Rhodes wrote. “But I’d rather be in control of the narrative instead of leaving the [social media] trolls to their speculation.” Explore more on these topics Alaska Wildlife Running Marathon Animals news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/26/at-l.text: At least six people were killed and multiple people were injured in Russian strikes across Ukraine over the past day, according to local authorities.In Zaporizhzhia Oblast in southeastern Ukraine, two women died and seven people were injured following attacks on the region, regional governor Ivan Fedorov reported on Saturday morning."A total of 86 reports were received of damage to infrastructure, residential buildings, and vehicles," he wrote in a post on Telegram.Two people were also killed and eight were injured in Donetsk in eastern Ukraine, governor Vadym Filashkin said, with 1,121 people evacuated from the front lines.In Kherson Oblast, Oleksandr Prokudin, the head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration, reported that another person was killed and three people were injured in attacks across the region."Russian forces struck critical and social infrastructure, as well as residential neighborhoods in the region’s settlements, damaging five private homes in particular. The occupiers also destroyed private vehicles," Prokudin said.A 69-year-old man was also killed in a drone strike on the Sumy region in the north of the country, according to local authorities. A further 10 people were wounded in a guided aerial bomb attack on the region.Russian forces also carried out another wave of strikes on the Ukrainian capital overnight, injuring five people, per Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.The Ukrainian air force said early Saturday that Russia had launched 173 attack drones at Ukraine overnight."According to preliminary data, as of 7:30 am, air defense forces have shot down or neutralised 134 enemy UAVs of the Shahed and Gerber types, as well as other types of drones," the force said, adding that strikes were recorded at 19 locations.On Saturday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Russia had also carried out a "double strike" attack on a logistics facility serving fast-food chain McDonald’s."Relentless attacks disrupt Ukrainians’ daily lives, damage businesses, threaten jobs, and undermine international investment," he wrote in a post on social media, while also sharing video footage appearing to show the aftermath of the strikes.Putin denies plans for conflict with Europe amid rising tensionsIt comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin told reporters in Saint Petersburg that Moscow was not preparing for conflict with Europe, despite warnings from European officials amid an increasing number of suspected Russian hybrid attacks."We are not preparing for any kind of hostilities with Europe," the Russian leader said. "There is no real motive to escalate the situation with Europe, no matter what anyone says, no matter who says it, including in the Baltic states".Sitting on NATO's eastern flank, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are particularly vulnerable to security threats stemming from Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In recent months, the three Baltic states have seen a rapidly growing number of drone incursions and related incidents, raising fresh concerns over airspace security and prompting Brussels to step up efforts to coordinate Europe's response.
